scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Putting things in order is a job every program needs. Today we learn Python's two sorting tools.

scenes.onScreen: "Two ways to sort": three numbered lines (1. list.sort() reorders the list itself; 2. sorted(list) returns a new sorted list; 3. key= sorts by a rule, reverse=True flips the order) and an analogy card: lining up students by height: you can reorder the real line, or just write down a sorted copy on paper
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Python has two ways to sort. The sort method reorders the list itself, in place, and returns nothing. The sorted function leaves the original alone, and gives you a new sorted list. Think of lining up students by height. You can move the real students, or you can write a sorted copy on paper. Reverse equals True flips the order. And key lets you sort by a rule.

lines: sorted(list) returns a new sorted list

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: sort returns None
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; wrong code shakes; the Python error lines appear in tomato; the fix slides in and the terminal turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We sort the list and save the result. We print it, and get None. Sort changes the list in place, and returns nothing, just like append. If you want a new sorted list to save, use the sorted function. Or call sort on its own line, and keep using the original list.

props.why: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None, so saving its result gives None; use sorted() when you want a new list back.

shorts.title: Sort in place
shorts.hook: "The sort method puts a list in order, right where it is."
shorts.script: The sort method puts a list in order, right where it is. Nums dot sort, with brackets, and the list is reordered, smallest to biggest. The same list object changes. Sort returns nothing, so you do not save its result. Use it when you do not need the old order any more, and you want the list itself sorted. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Reorder the list.

shorts.title: Sorted makes a copy
shorts.script: The sorted function is different. It takes any list, and gives you a new sorted list. The original stays in its old order. Use it when you need both the old and the new order. Also use it for a sorted view for printing. Add reverse equals True, and the biggest item comes first. Sorted never changes the original. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: A new sorted list.

shorts.title: Sort by a rule
shorts.hook: "The key option sorts by a rule."
shorts.script: The key option sorts by a rule. Sorted of words, key equals len, sorts words by their length. Fig has three letters, apple five, banana six. Python measures each word with len, then sorts by those numbers. Notice there are no brackets after len. You hand Python the tool, and Python uses it on each item in turn. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Sort by length.

shorts.title: Sort returns None
shorts.script: Another None bug. You write result equals nums dot sort, and print the result. It says None. Sort changes the list in place and returns nothing, just like append. If you want a new sorted list to save, use the sorted function instead. Or call sort on its own line, and keep using the same list name afterwards. Keep coding, says Xecxec!
shorts.caption: Use sorted to save.

shorts.title: Pun and challenge
shorts.script: Why was the list so organised? It always knew its place in line. Your challenge. Take the list sixty four, ninety one, seventy two, eighty eight. Sort it from the highest to the lowest. Print the result. You should see ninety one first. Try it with sort, and then with sorted. Which one is easier to print? Tell us in the comments. Keep coding, says Xecxec! Full video: EP 30.
